analysis.one_liner: Gives nannies, housekeepers, and home care aides written contracts, paid sick days, overtime, and rest breaks.
analysis.headline: The Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act, introduced with 131 cosponsors in June 2024, never received a committee hearing or floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend basic workplace rights to the roughly 2.2 million people who clean homes, care for children, and look after seniors and people with disabilities in private homes. It would require written work agreements, earned paid sick time, meal and rest breaks, advance notice of schedule changes, and overtime pay for live-in workers, and it would let these workers sue for discrimination under federal civil rights law, a protection most are currently excluded from because of their small household employers. The bill was referred to six House committees, none of which acted on it, and it never came up for a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic workers — nannies, housekeepers, home health and personal care aides — who are disproportionately women of color and immigrants, earn an average of about $13.79 an hour, and are largely excluded from federal overtime, anti-discrimination, and collective bargaining protections. They would gain written contracts, up to 56 hours a year of earned paid sick time, guaranteed meal and rest breaks, 72-hour notice of schedule changes, overtime pay for live-in workers, protection from retaliation (including threats to report immigration status), and access to Title VII discrimination protections. Families who depend on their care would also benefit from lower turnover and better continuity of care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic workers, mostly low-paid women of color

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers of domestic workers (those working 8+ hours a week) to provide a signed written agreement in plain language covering pay rate, schedule, breaks, termination policy, and grievance procedures, and bars such agreements from containing pre-dispute arbitration clauses or NDAs that limit the worker's rights.

Gives domestic workers one hour of earned paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for their own illness, caring for family, or dealing with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

Repeals the Fair Labor Standards Act exemption that has kept live-in domestic workers outside overtime pay requirements since 1974, and gives live-in workers terminated without cause written notice plus 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance pay.

Guarantees a 30-minute meal break after 5 hours and paid 10-minute rest breaks every 4 hours, 72-hour advance written notice of schedule changes with partial pay for late cancellations, and protection of workers' private communications and living space from employer monitoring.

Extends Title VII civil rights protections against discrimination to domestic employees, who are currently de facto excluded because of small-employer thresholds and misclassification as independent contractors, and makes retaliation — including threatening to report a worker's immigration status — unlawful, with a presumption of retaliation for adverse actions within 90 days of a worker asserting rights.

The bill's findings note domestic workers average about $13.79 an hour, less than 2% have retirement benefits, 65% lack health insurance, and private homes are among the industries with the highest rates of wage and labor law violations.

analysis.who_pays: Household employers — including middle-income families who regularly hire a nanny, housekeeper, or aide — would bear new obligations: written agreements, record-keeping, paid sick time, break compliance, and schedule-change pay. Wealthier households with live-in staff would face overtime costs and severance or lodging requirements on termination. Home care agencies and app-based domestic work platforms would face compliance costs and lose practices like wage deductions for cancellations and mandatory arbitration clauses. The federal government would pick up a temporary increase in the Medicaid matching rate to help state-funded programs absorb the new standards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Household employers, care agencies, and platforms

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls on ordinary household employers, not just agencies: any family employing a babysitter, nanny, or cleaner for 8 or more hours a week would have to produce signed written agreements covering a long list of required terms, keep records for at least 3 years, and pay for late schedule changes, which could push some families toward casual, off-the-books arrangements that leave workers with no protections at all.

The bill authorizes a temporary increase in the federal Medicaid matching rate to help cover the cost of applying the standards to Medicaid-funded home care, adding federal spending during a period when the program's finances are already strained.

Applying federal employment standards inside private homes raises enforcement questions unique to this workforce — the bill itself acknowledges that isolation, immigration status, and fear of losing the job kept 91% of workers with complaints from raising them — so new rights on paper may reach fewer workers than intended without the bill's outreach grants and hotline being funded.

The written-agreement ban on mandatory arbitration and nondisclosure terms would strip household employers of tools they currently use to keep disputes private, a real cost to employers even if supporters view it as necessary given the isolation of the workforce.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core case is strong: this workforce is nearly unique in modern American labor law for how completely it was left out — no overtime for live-in workers, de facto exclusion from federal anti-discrimination law, and among the highest rates of wage theft — while the work itself (child care, elder care, home care) keeps the rest of the economy running. The main honest cost is that the rules land on household employers, including middle-income families, not just companies, and the paperwork and paid-leave requirements are real burdens for them; a small share of families may respond by hiring informally, which would hurt the very workers the bill protects. Design features like the 8-hour-a-week threshold, the 56-hour sick-time cap, and delayed enforcement for government-funded programs show an effort to moderate that burden.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2024 and sent to six House committees, but none of them took it up, no vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act on June 13, 2024, and it was referred the same day to the Education and the Workforce Committee plus five other committees (House Administration, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight, and Judiciary).
131 House members cosponsored the bill — every one of them a Democrat, with no Republican support.
The action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind after the initial referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without ever reaching a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of domestic workers — including households with live-in staff, home care agencies, and app-based care platforms — are better off because the bill died: they avoided new wage, scheduling, paid-sick-time, contract, and anti-retaliation obligations. Domestic workers, an estimated 2.2 million mostly low-paid women of color and immigrants, gained nothing and remain outside federal overtime, anti-discrimination, and benefits protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Household employers, care agencies, and platforms

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act on June 13, 2024, with a detailed bill laying out contracts, paid sick time, overtime, and anti-discrimination protections for domestic workers.

for.name: 131 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill; no Republican joined.

against.name: House Republican leadership

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before any of its six assigned committees for a markup or to the House floor for a vote during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 131 cosponsors were Democrats, and with Republicans holding the House majority in the 118th Congress, the bill never advanced past its initial committee referral.

industries.note: Agencies placing nannies, housekeepers, and aides would have to comply with written-contract, paid-sick-time, break, scheduling, and record-keeping rules, and would lose the ability to require arbitration clauses or deduct wages for late cancellations. The bill's own findings list private-home employment among the industries with the highest rates of labor law violations, which is the gap these rules target.

App-based platforms that connect households with cleaners and caregivers would face new obligations, including a ban on penalizing workers who communicate directly with customers instead of through the platform, and a ban on mandatory arbitration clauses in work agreements. Platforms whose business model relies on contractor classification could face claims from workers treated as employees.

industries.industry: Wealthy households employing live-in domestic staff
industries.note: The bill repeals the 1974 Fair Labor Standards Act exemption that has kept live-in domestic workers outside overtime rules since 1974, and requires 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance when a live-in worker is terminated. These costs fall almost entirely on households wealthy enough to employ live-in staff.

industries.industry: Medicaid-funded home and community-based care providers
industries.note: The bill temporarily increases the federal Medicaid matching rate for services provided by domestic employees, so state-funded home care programs get help absorbing the new wage and benefit standards. Providers and the seniors and people with disabilities they serve both benefit from a more stable, better-paid workforce.
